extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; critics and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging lyric poetry and literary prose, focused on qualities such as musicality, simplicity of feeling, tonal control, and the relation of wit and satire to thought. Geared toward critical assessment rather than creative instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality / twin melody of lyrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrics should be fundamentally musical; each song-like poem ought to suggest or contain a melody, as if 'each must have a twin melody born in the same moment and by the same inspiration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes that Heine's finest products are 'songs' and that in reading them 'we feel as if each must have a twin melody.' Evaluate lyric poems for intrinsic rhythmic and musical quality, sense of singability, and close relation between language and tune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy of expression that can 'indicate a whole sad history in a single quatrain' is prized; a brief lyric may evoke a vast emotional scene with very few words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for poems that achieve depth through compression — minimal images or lines that conjure extensive narrative or feeling. The exemplar: a quatrain that is 'beautiful, simple, and perfect as a “big round tear.”' Lack of unnecessary images or thoughts is a mark of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple, natural pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest power in lyric poetry lies in 'simple pathos' and the natural expression of tender emotions rather than elaborate intellectualism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether emotion feels genuine and unforced; compare to the example that Heine's songs are 'all music and feeling' and 'pure feeling, breathed in pure music.' Avoid poems whose pathos feels contrived or overwrought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative representation without artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling may be expressed imaginatively—by a brief cameo-image, mysterious dream, or dramatized little-story—but must not give a sense of artificiality; development should feel 'by the same beautiful necessity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value versatility of form (cameo, dream, ballad, idyl) when images and narratives arise organically. The critic praises Heine's use of brief images and little stories that never feel forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled tonal contrast and sudden fall
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful transition from the lofty to the ludicrous (a sudden fall) is an effective poetic device, but it requires careful control of reader emotion and expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet's ability to 'poise our emotion and expectation at such a height as to give effect to the sudden fall.' This technique is praised when done by a poet who manages tone (Heine's use cited); when mishandled it becomes jarring rather than humorous or illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightness combined with precision (prose style)
rubrics_metrics.description: In prose, an 'airy lightness' paired with precision of touch is a desirable quality—writing that is lively without sacrificing exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique prose for economy, clarity, and deftness: being facile or gushing without precise handling is a fault. The essay attributes to Heine both 'airy lightness, yet precision of touch.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and balance in satire and praise
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic or satirist ideally distributes both satire and appreciation impartially, avoiding party zeal or unwavering partisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay commends Heine's 'impartiality which made his less favorable critics... charge him with reckless caprice and venality'—use this as guidance to value balanced judgment that can satirize faults without wholesale denunciation of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unscrupulous personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarseness and 'unscrupulous personalities' are reproachable; satire should not descend into gratuitous personal vilification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between acceptable satirical critique of foibles and reprehensible personal insinuations. The essay censures Heine's caricature of Madame Wohl and scurrilous insinuations as 'utterly inexcusable.' This is an anti-pattern for the critic/poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor that grows organically from thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and humor are most successful when they 'grow out of a rich loam of thought' rather than being superficial or merely glib.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humorous writing for intellectual grounding and organic development; the essay cites 'Deutschland' as charming because its humor arises from substantive thought rather than mere frivolity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of originality and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly original, fantastic works may be admirable for imagination but can 'strain the imagination' and be less generally popular; there is a trade-off between originality and broad appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether inventive, fantastic elements enhance the work's effect or overburden the reader. 'Atta Troll' is praised for originality yet noted as too great a strain to be a general favorite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope for poetical temperament (short vs sustained forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poets are 'too impressible and mercurial for any sustained production'; their powers are best shown in short lyrics rather than long, sustained works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the poet's temperament suits the chosen form: mercurial lyricists may excel in brief songs but falter in longer poems, which demand steadier weight and force ('Heine is too impressible... for any sustained production').

rubrics_metrics.name: Finished simplicity and rhythmic grace
rubrics_metrics.description: A finished simplicity together with rhythmic grace are stylistic ideals; lyric should combine polished simplicity with musical rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast lyrical lightness with deeper thought: the essay notes both Goethe and Heine have 'masterly, finished simplicity and rhythmic grace,' but Goethe's has more mingled thought/feeling and greater weight. Evaluate both grace and substantive depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should target the caricature, not the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective satire laughs at the poor reflection ('the caricature') of great ideas, not at the ideas themselves ('not at the god').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing satirical work, determine whether the target is a distorted embodiment of an idea (legitimate) rather than the idea or virtue itself (misplaced). The essay's metaphor about mirrors that make Apollo a caricature illustrates this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about patronage to avoid charges of venality
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's openness about receiving patronage or stipends can vindicate them from accusations of venality; concealment invites suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes Heine 'has never attempted to conceal the reception of that stipend' and finds his explanation a 'sufficient vindication.' For authors/journalists, disclosure and candid explanation of financial ties is a recommended practice to maintain credibility.
